title: Synthesis answer
$comment: Added after the v1 freeze; see schema/CHANGES.md for the case that forced it. Uses the keyword subset implemented by tools/validate.py; an unknown keyword is an error there, never ignored.
description: Cheapest whole-contract sizes over several candidate instruments meeting a stated objective, or a certificate that none exist. SEPARATE from a result, and a different question: a result answers 'do THESE terms, costs and holdings satisfy my objective', about a proposal that already names its legs and their sizes, and its `size_windows` is the one-leg special case. A synthesis answers 'what sizes WOULD satisfy it, over these instruments' -- its input is a set of candidates and an objective, and its output is sizes that do not exist yet. The document carries the QUESTION as well as the answer, because a checker that re-added the numbers the solver emitted would be confirming arithmetic rather than verifying a claim. It carries NO solver state: no tableau, no pivot order, no basis. A certificate that needed the search replayed would not be a certificate.

request.description: The question, in full. Everything a checker needs to rebuild the same program.

base.description: What the holder already has. May be empty: synthesising from nothing is a legitimate question.

candidates.description: The instruments offered, one unit each. `price` is what one contract costs, a hypothetical per-unit price rather than a book walk: a synthesis asks what size to buy, and the size is what a walk needs before it can price anything. A depth-priced answer is the size window's question, per leg, on a size already chosen.

lot.description: The whole-contract increment sizes are rounded to. One when absent.

status.description: `feasible`: sizes were found and re-checked against the objective. `infeasible`: the RELAXATION is infeasible, so no whole-contract answer exists either, and `certificate` proves it. `rounding_failed`: the relaxation was feasible and no rounding of it met the objective -- a statement about this search, never about existence.

sizes.description: Present exactly when `status` is `feasible`. Whole contracts, named by candidate rather than by position.

cost.description: What the reported sizes cost, present with `sizes`.

relaxed.description: The linear program's own answer, before rounding. Carried with `feasible` and with `rounding_failed`, so a reader sees how far the rounding moved and, when it failed, what it was rounding.

certificate.description: Present exactly when `status` is `infeasible`. A Farkas certificate: non-negative weights on the constraint rows with `A^T y <= 0` and `b . y > 0`, which is exactly the statement that no non-negative sizes satisfy the rows. The checker verifies it by one multiplication, never by re-solving.

weights.description: Sparse, and each weight NAMES ITS SITE. A bare vector would be ordered by the rows, making row order an implicit contract between three implementations; naming the site lets a checker look it up among its own rows, so order stops mattering and a site the checker cannot find is a refusal rather than a silent misalignment. Sparse because a Farkas certificate is: PLAN section 3's uses two rows out of ten.

side.description: Which constraint at that price: `at` is the value there, `above` and `below` are the limits from either side of it. A jump makes the three different numbers, and a sloped piece attains its infimum only in the limit.
